sections.title: Mission · Connect and Troubleshoot a Linux Host
paragraphs: A Linux computer needs basic network configuration to communicate. Understand networks, routers, IP addresses, DNS client configuration, hostname resolution, interfaces, routes, and basic troubleshooting.
bullets: route, ip route show, ifconfig, and ip addr show

sections.title: What Is a Network?
paragraphs: A network connects devices so they can exchange data and share services. A local network can connect onward to other networks and the Internet.

sections.title: The Internet
paragraphs: The Internet is a global network of interconnected networks. A computer typically reaches it through a local network and router.
sections.callout: COMPUTER → LOCAL NETWORK → ROUTER → OTHER NETWORKS

sections.title: Router
paragraphs: A router forwards traffic between networks and selects a path toward remote destinations.

sections.title: IPv4
paragraphs: IPv4 addresses are commonly written as four decimal octets separated by dots, such as 192.168.20.10.

sections.title: IPv6
paragraphs: IPv6 addresses use hexadecimal groups separated by colons and provide a much larger address space.

sections.title: Network Interfaces
paragraphs: A network interface connects the host to a network and can have link state, addresses, and other configuration.

sections.title: ifconfig
paragraphs: ifconfig is the traditional utility for viewing and configuring network interfaces.

sections.title: ip addr show
paragraphs: ip addr show is the modern command for displaying interfaces and their addresses.
sections.callout: ip addr show = MY INTERFACES AND ADDRESSES

sections.title: ifconfig vs. ip addr show
paragraphs: Both expose interface information. ifconfig is traditional, while ip addr show belongs to the modern ip toolset.

sections.title: Routing Table
paragraphs: The routing table tells the system where to send packets for different destination networks.

sections.title: route
paragraphs: route is the traditional command for viewing routing information.

sections.title: ip route show
paragraphs: ip route show is the modern command for displaying the routing table.
sections.callout: ip route show = SHOW ROUTING TABLE

sections.title: Exam Trap · Interface vs. Route
paragraphs: Interface and address information answers who the host is on a network. Routing information answers where traffic should be sent.
sections.callout: ADDRESS = WHO AM I? · ROUTE = WHERE DO I SEND IT?

sections.title: Default Route
paragraphs: The default route is the fallback path used when no more specific route matches, often pointing toward the router for other networks.

sections.title: DNS
paragraphs: The Domain Name System resolves human-readable names to network addresses and can also perform other lookups.

sections.title: /etc/resolv.conf
paragraphs: /etc/resolv.conf stores DNS client resolver configuration, including which DNS servers the host should query.

sections.title: /etc/hosts
paragraphs: /etc/hosts stores local static name-to-IP mappings that the computer already knows.

sections.title: Exam Trap · resolv.conf vs. hosts

table.caption: Ask a resolver or use a local mapping

sections.callout: RESOLV = WHO SHOULD I ASK? · HOSTS = I ALREADY KNOW THIS ONE

sections.title: host
paragraphs: host performs DNS lookups for a name or address.

sections.title: ping
paragraphs: ping tests basic network reachability using ICMP echo messages.

sections.title: Exam Trap · Ping Limitation
paragraphs: A failed ping does not automatically prove the remote device is down. Firewalls or policies may block ICMP while other services still work.

sections.title: netstat
paragraphs: netstat is a traditional utility for displaying network connections, listening sockets, and related network status.

sections.title: ss
paragraphs: ss is a modern utility for displaying socket information.

sections.title: Exam Trap · netstat vs. ss
paragraphs: Both help inspect network connections and sockets. netstat is traditional; ss is the modern socket utility.

sections.title: Basic LAN Requirements
bullets: DNS configuration when names are used

sections.title: Troubleshooting by Symptom
paragraphs: Check interface and address data, then routes, then name resolution, then reachability and socket state. The symptom determines which evidence to inspect first.

entries.title: Address vs. Route
paragraphs: ip addr show displays interface addresses; ip route show displays where traffic goes.

entries.title: DNS Config vs. Static Mapping
paragraphs: resolv.conf configures resolvers; hosts contains local mappings.

entries.title: ping vs. host
paragraphs: ping tests reachability; host performs DNS lookup.

entries.title: netstat vs. ss
paragraphs: Both inspect network/socket state; netstat is traditional and ss is modern.

entries.title: IPv4 vs. IPv6
paragraphs: IPv4 uses decimal dots; IPv6 uses hexadecimal colons.
